analysis.one_liner: Applies the Social Security payroll tax to all earnings and boosts retiree cost-of-living adjustments.
analysis.headline: A bill that would have raised Social Security cost-of-living adjustments and applied the program's payroll tax to all earnings, phasing out the cap between 2025 and 2031, died in committee with 3 cosponsors and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made two changes to Social Security. First, it would calculate annual cost-of-living increases using a price index that tracks what people 62 and older actually buy, which typically rises faster than the index used now, meaning bigger yearly benefit increases [S2]. Second, it would apply the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax to every dollar of wages and self-employment income, phasing in between 2025 and 2031; today, earnings above the annual cap (about $168,600 in 2024) are not taxed at all [S2]. High earners would get a small benefit credit for those extra taxes, but at very low rates (3% and 0.25%) that return far less than they pay in [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security retirees, survivors, and disabled beneficiaries. The new elderly-specific price index would produce larger annual cost-of-living increases, with the biggest gains going to older beneficiaries whose costs — especially health care — rise faster than the general index. The bill would also direct more payroll tax revenue into the trust funds, extending how long benefits can be paid in full. Low-income beneficiaries are explicitly protected: any benefit increase could not count against them for SSI or Medicaid eligibility [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security retirees and disabled beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Cost-of-living adjustments would be recalculated using the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, an index the Bureau of Labor Statistics would publish tracking the spending of households headed by someone 62 or older, which generally rises faster than the index used today — producing larger annual benefit increases.

The bill makes clear that any benefit increase from the new index cannot be counted as income or resources when determining eligibility for Supplemental Security Income or Medicaid, so the poorest beneficiaries would not lose other aid because their Social Security check grew.

Starting in 2025, the Social Security payroll tax would apply to earnings above the annual cap, phasing in from 86% of above-cap earnings to 100% by 2031, for both employees and the self-employed — directing substantial new revenue into a program facing a funding shortfall.

High earners would not pay the new taxes entirely without credit: earnings above the cap would count in the benefit formula at low marginal rates (3% then 0.25%), a nod to keeping some link between contributions and benefits.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and self-employed people whose earnings exceed the annual taxable cap — roughly the top 6% of earners — would pay the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax (or their share plus their employer's match) on all their income, phased in from 2025 through 2031. Employers of high earners would pay the matching 6.2% on wages above the cap. High earners would receive a small added benefit in return, but at far less than 1-to-1 [S2].

drawbacks.text: It is a large tax increase on high earners: someone with wages well above the cap would eventually owe the full 12.4% Social Security tax on every dollar, while the benefit formula credits those extra contributions at only 3% and then 0.25% — they would pay in far more than they would ever get back, weakening the traditional link between what you contribute and what you receive.

Because the elderly price index generally rises faster than the index currently used, annual cost-of-living increases would grow faster and compound over time, increasing program costs on top of the new revenue — a cost trajectory an honest supporter must acknowledge.

The phase-in schedule would create a multi-year transition in which some high earners face rising marginal payroll tax rates year by year, complicating payroll compliance for employers with highly paid staff.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and durable: larger, more accurate cost-of-living increases for tens of millions of beneficiaries, protection for the poorest against losing SSI and Medicaid, and a major new revenue stream for a program that faces a financing gap. The costs fall on a narrow group — earners above roughly $168,600, who would pay noticeably more in taxes while receiving only a token benefit increase. That is a deliberate design choice, not a flaw: the bill is built to fund and expand Social Security on the backs of the highest earners. The main honest objection is fairness to that group and the faster spending growth from the richer index.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee — it was sent to the Social Security subcommittee in December 2024 and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jill Tokuda introduced the bill on August 2, 2024, with two Democratic cosponsors, near the end of a session with little legislative runway left.
It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, plus the Energy and Commerce and Education and the Workforce committees — a three-committee referral that splits jurisdiction and makes action harder.
On December 17, 2024, it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security, a step that normally precedes a hearing, not a vote.
No further action was taken; the bill never reached the House floor, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the payroll tax cap — roughly the top 6% of earners — and their employers, who would have owed Social Security tax on every dollar of above-cap wages starting in 2025, are better off because the bill never moved. Beneficiaries gained nothing because the richer cost-of-living formula never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the payroll tax cap

for.name: Rep. Jill Tokuda
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 2, 2024, to expand Social Security benefits and tax all earnings above the payroll cap.

for.name: Reps. Steve Cohen and Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsors; both were listed as original sponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Committee chair controls the markup calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it was sent to the Social Security subcommittee on December 17, 2024, and no further action followed before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with Republicans chairing Ways and Means the bill never advanced.

industries.note: Would owe the full Social Security payroll tax on all earnings, phased in through 2031, while the benefit formula credits those extra contributions at only 3% and 0.25% — a small fraction of what they pay. This is the group the bill's funding is drawn from.
Employers pay a matching 6.2% Social Security tax, so companies with highly paid executives and professionals would face a new tax on all above-cap wages, raising the cost of top-end compensation.

Self-employed people pay both halves of the payroll tax (the full 12.4%), so above-cap net earnings from law, medicine, finance, and other practices would eventually be fully taxed with no corresponding benefit.
